The Cap Seller and the Monkeys
Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
A Journey to the Magical Mountains

topics.name: Living & non-living: is the distinction real?
sub: The usual 'signs of life': moves, breathes, eats, grows, responds, makes babies, gets rid of waste
Tricky cases that break the list: fire (eats, breathes oxygen, grows, spreads), a 100-year-old dormant seed, growing crystals, a plucked flower, a dead leaf, a virus
J.C. Bose: plants respond to touch, injury and poison; he claimed metals also 'tire' and 'recover'
Everything is made of elements forged in stars
Is a handful of soil living or non-living?
topics.summary: We start by sorting things at home into 'alive' and 'not alive' and writing down why. Then we test those reasons on tricky cases. Fire eats, breathes and grows; is it alive? A seed can sit still for 100 years and then sprout; was it alive all that time? Crystals grow. Then we meet J.C. Bose, who built machines sensitive enough to show plants reacting, and who argued that even metals show tiredness and recovery. We end with the honest truth: scientists still do not have one agreed definition of life. NASA's working definition is 'a self-sustaining chemical system capable of evolution', and even that is argued over.
topics.oneness: If the same atoms move from stars to rocks to plants to me, at what moment does something become 'alive'? Is aliveness a line, or a gradient?

res.title: A Seed Is Sleepy, Dianna Hutts Aston
Acharya J.C. Bose Indian Botanic Garden, Howrah
The Private Life of Plants (BBC, David Attenborough)
The King's Doubt: full game (cards + parent guide)

topics.name: How did life begin?
sub: Earth began hot, with no life
The oldest evidence of life is about 3.5 billion years old (stromatolites: layered rocks built by microbes)
First life was tiny single cells in water
Ideas: Darwin's 'warm little pond', deep-sea hot vents, life arriving from space (panspermia), the 'RNA world'
Miller–Urey experiment (1952): gases + electric sparks made amino acids
Nobody has made life from scratch yet
topics.summary: We tell Earth's story on a long rope or saree: Earth forms, it is too hot for life, then early on the first tiny cells appear in water, and humans arrive only in the last few millimetres. We look at photos of stromatolites, rocks built layer by layer by microbes over billions of years, some still growing in Australia today. Then we lay out the main ideas scientists have about how life started, and the one honest answer: nobody knows yet. Scientists have made some building blocks of life in a lab, but never life itself.
topics.oneness: If life came from non-living chemicals, was it ever really separate from them?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
NASA Space Place: life in the universe

topics.name: What's common between living and non-living?
sub: Everything is made of atoms; about 90 kinds occur naturally (elements)
The body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen
The same carbon is in pencil lead, diamond, bread and you
Atoms are recycled: the water you drink has passed through clouds, rivers, plants and animals
Stars made most elements: 'we are star stuff'
topics.summary: We ask what a rock, a tree and a child have in common, and find that underneath they are built from the same tiny pieces: atoms. Your body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, the same elements found in air, water and coal. Carbon in a pencil and carbon in a diamond are the same atom arranged differently. Atoms never wear out; they keep moving between rocks, air, plants and people. Most of them were made inside stars long before Earth existed. So the difference between living and non-living is not in what they are made of, but in how those pieces are arranged and behave.
topics.oneness: If my atoms were once a star and will one day be soil, which part of the journey is 'me'?

res.title: Older Than the Stars, Karen C. Fox
PhET: Build an Atom (simulation)

topics.name: Materials around me & their properties
sub: Properties: hard/soft, rough/smooth, heavy/light, bendy/stiff, strong/brittle, see-through/opaque, magnetic/not
Float or sink: not about heavy vs light but about how tightly packed (Archimedes)
Microscope views: salt crystals, sugar, cloth threads, hair, soil
Soil & rocks: sand, clay, loam; soil layers; soil is full of life (a teaspoon holds billions of microbes)
Surprising 'materials': is water a material? Tears? Shadow? Sound? Fire?
topics.summary: Children become material detectives: touching, bending, dropping and floating everyday things and describing them with exact words. Float-or-sink predictions surprise them: a heavy steel plate floats when shaped like a bowl, while a tiny pebble sinks. We look closer with a magnifier or phone microscope: salt is little cubes, cloth is woven threads. We dig into soil, see its layers settle in a jar, and learn that one spoonful of good soil contains more living microbes than there are people on Earth, so is soil living? Finally the big puzzle: water and tears are matter, but a shadow is only missing light, sound is a shaking that travels through matter, and fire is hot glowing gas. What counts as 'stuff'?
topics.oneness: Is soil a thing, or a crowd of living beings? Where does the material end and the living begin?

res.title: Arvind Gupta Toys: science from everyday junk
PhET: Density (float or sink)

topics.name: Kinds of living things
sub: Plants: root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed; what plants need (water, light, air, soil nutrients); grow-a-seed
Fungi: mushrooms, mould, yeast; neither plant nor animal, closer to animals than to plants
Animals: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects and other invertebrates
Microbes (links to B3)
Humans are animals: mammals and primates
Groups are made by humans, and they keep changing
topics.summary: We meet the big families of life. Plants: we find the parts on a real plant and discover which parts we eat (carrot is a root, potato is a stem, spinach a leaf, cauliflower a flower, rice a seed), then start growing seeds in light and dark to see what plants need. Fungi surprise everyone: mushrooms are not plants, and DNA shows fungi are closer relatives of animals. We sort animals by features (fur, feathers, scales, backbone or not) and place humans honestly among them: we are mammals, we are animals. Finally we see that these groups are human-made boxes: scientists used to call fungi plants, and today most scientists say birds are living dinosaurs.
topics.oneness: Who drew these boxes, and does nature know about them? If a mushroom is more like me than a plant, what does 'like me' mean?

res.title: A Seed Is Sleepy, Dianna Hutts Aston
StoryWeaver (Pratham Books): free picture books on plants and animals
Any botanical garden, e.g. Lalbagh, Bengaluru

topics.name: Big Bang & the universe
sub: About 13.8 billion years ago the universe was tiny, hot and dense, and began expanding
First atoms: hydrogen and helium
Mass and gravity: gravity pulls matter into clumps → stars, planets, galaxies, clusters
Stars make heavier elements and scatter them when they explode
Black holes; dark matter and dark energy (about 95% of the universe is something we cannot see)
Our planet: about 71% water, 29% land
topics.summary: We tell the biggest story there is. Long ago everything was squeezed into an unimaginably small, hot speck, which grew and is still growing, like dots on a balloon moving apart as it inflates. As it cooled, the first atoms appeared. Mass pulls on mass; that pull is gravity, and gravity gathered gas into stars and stars into galaxies. Stars cook new elements and scatter them when they explode; our Earth, and we, are made from that dust. Then the mysteries: black holes so strong that light cannot escape, and the shocking fact that most of the universe is 'dark' stuff no one has ever seen. We also learn how ideas about gravity changed: Newton said it is a pulling force, and it worked for 200 years; Einstein showed mass bends space and time itself; and today some scientists think even Einstein's idea needs fixing.
topics.oneness: If everything came from one tiny point, is the universe one thing that became many?

res.title: NASA Space Place
Me and My Place in Space, Joan Sweeney
Nehru Planetarium (Delhi / Mumbai)

topics.name: My world: how humans live, and why
sub: My world: home, food, transport, money, work, school, festivals
The chain of people behind my breakfast
Humans are social animals: families, groups, rules, sharing, trade
Why we live like this: biology (we bond, cooperate, compete), environment, history, culture
Different people live in different worlds: village, city, forest, another country
Money: from barter to coins to digital
topics.summary: We begin with the child's own world: list everything used in one day and trace where it came from. A single breakfast needs farmers, drivers, shopkeepers and cooks; no human lives alone. We ask why humans live in families and groups: like elephants, wolves and ants, we survive by cooperating, and our bodies are wired to bond (a hug really changes brain chemicals). We see that a child in a forest village, a fishing town or a city in another country lives in a different 'world' with different food, work and rules. We play a barter market to see why money was invented. And we ask the old question honestly: are humans naturally selfish or naturally kind? Thinkers disagree.
topics.oneness: If my breakfast needs a hundred people, where do 'I' end and 'we' begin?

res.title: StoryWeaver: stories of children across India

topics.name: The world of microorganisms
sub: Too small to see: bacteria, yeast and other fungi, amoebas, algae; viruses (alive or not?)
Everywhere: soil, air, water, skin, gut
Helpers: curd, idli/dosa batter, bread, compost; ocean plankton make about half of Earth's oxygen
Some make us sick (links to C10)
Leeuwenhoek first saw them in the 1670s with a home-made lens
topics.summary: There is a whole hidden world all around and inside us. We hear how a Dutch cloth-seller, Leeuwenhoek, ground tiny lenses and was the first person to see 'little animals' swimming in a drop of water. Microbes turn milk into curd, make idli batter rise, rot leaves into soil and, through tiny ocean plankton, make about half the oxygen we breathe. Only a few make us sick. We make curd at home and watch yeast blow up a balloon. And we ask whether viruses are alive: they cannot do anything outside a living cell, so scientists still disagree.
topics.oneness: If tiny beings make my curd, my soil and my oxygen, how separate is my life from theirs?

res.title: Microcosmos (1996 film)
Arvind Gupta Toys: simple magnifiers

topics.name: Other beings' worlds: how a bird sees the world
sub: Every creature lives in its own world of senses (umwelt, Jakob von Uexküll, 1909)
Birds see ultraviolet and have 4 kinds of colour cones (we have 3)
Many birds sense Earth's magnetic field to migrate; Amur falcons fly from East Asia through Nagaland to Africa
Bird societies: flocks, nests, parents, songs with local 'dialects', crows remember faces and use tools
Seeing time: many birds and insects see fast movements we miss
(Series can continue: an ant's world, a dog's world, a fish's world…)
topics.summary: Our world of cars, money and roads is only one world. A crow on the same street lives in a different one. Birds see colours we cannot even imagine, including ultraviolet patterns on flowers and feathers. Many feel the Earth's magnetism and use it like a compass to fly thousands of kilometres; the Amur falcon crosses the Arabian Sea on its way from Asia to Africa. Birds have families, neighbours, quarrels and songs, and crows can remember a human face for years. We try to imagine life in a bird's world, and meet a famous question: can we ever truly know what it is like to be another creature?
topics.oneness: If each being lives in its own world, is there one 'real' world, or many?

res.title: Planet Earth: Birds of Paradise episode (BBC)
Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary, Thattekad (Kerala) or a local lake

topics.name: Cycles in the sky & weather
sub: Day and night: Earth spins
A year: Earth goes around the Sun; seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun
Moon phases: we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half; the Moon makes no light of its own
India's six ritus and the monsoon
Clouds and rain: water evaporates, cools and condenses
Planets you can see (Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn) and stars as distant suns
topics.summary: With a torch and a ball we discover why day and night happen: the Earth spins, so our side faces the Sun and then turns away. Seasons come from Earth's tilt; most people wrongly think it is about being closer to the Sun. The Moon makes no light of its own; its shape changes because we see different amounts of its sunlit half, and the child keeps a moon diary for a month. We learn India's six ritus, why the monsoon comes, and make a cloud in a jar. We hear how ideas changed: people once believed the Sun went around the Earth; Aryabhata proposed in 499 CE that the Earth spins; Copernicus and Galileo argued the Earth goes around the Sun, and Galileo was put on trial for it.
topics.oneness: Sun, Moon, seasons and my sleep all move in cycles. Am I part of the sky's rhythm?

res.title: NASA Space Place: Moon phases
Shadow-stick sundial

topics.name: Forces, vibrations & sound
sub: Push and pull; gravity pulls everything down
The floor pushes back up (normal force); friction; air resistance; water pushes up (buoyancy); magnets
Contact forces are, at heart, electric pushes between electrons; your hand never truly 'touches' the table
Gravity is the exception, a different force
Sound is vibration travelling through air, water and solids; no sound in space
Loud/soft and high/low (pitch); echoes
topics.summary: Children push, pull, drop and float things to feel forces. The surprise: when you sit on a chair, the chair pushes back up, and when you 'touch' anything, its electrons and yours push each other away; atoms never really touch. Air pushes against a falling sheet of paper; water pushes up on a boat. We retell the history of falling: Aristotle said heavy things fall faster, and people believed him for nearly 2000 years until Galileo tested it; Newton explained gravity as a pull; Einstein explained it as bent space. Sound is also a push travelling along: we feel our throat buzz when humming Om, watch rice jump on a drum, and build a cup telephone.
topics.oneness: If nothing ever truly touches, how are we all still connected?

res.title: The Way Things Work Now, David Macaulay
PhET: Forces and Motion Basics
Arvind Gupta Toys: sound and force toys

topics.name: Light, colour & shadows
sub: Light sources: Sun, fire, bulbs, fireflies (living light)
We see when light bounces off things into our eyes
Light travels in straight lines → shadows; shadow size changes with distance
Reflection: mirrors, still water
White light holds all colours (rainbow, prism); objects show the colours they bounce back
Mixing paint vs mixing light: paints get darker; red, green and blue light make white
Darkness is the absence of light; light and shade in painting
topics.summary: Darkness is not a thing; it is what is left when light is missing. We make shadow puppets and discover shadows grow as hands move closer to the torch. We bounce torchlight off mirrors to hit a target, make rainbows with a glass of water, and learn that white light is all colours mixed, as Newton showed with a prism. A red apple looks red because it bounces red light and swallows the rest. Then the painting surprise: mixing paints makes colours darker, while mixing coloured light makes white. We paint a ball with one light source to see light, shade and shadow. And the deep puzzle: is light a wave or a particle? Scientists argued for centuries and now say it behaves as both, which still puzzles them.
topics.oneness: Is colour in the apple, in the light, or in my mind?

res.title: PhET: Color Vision
Shadow puppet show (Tholu Bommalata / Togalu Gombeyaata)

topics.name: Nature's events
sub: Rain and the water cycle
Floods, droughts and dry spells
Wind, storms and cyclones (countries around the Indian Ocean take turns naming them)
Thunder and lightning (light arrives before sound)
Earthquakes and tsunamis (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami)
Snow in the Himalayas
Why the monsoon happens: land heats faster than sea
topics.summary: Nature is always moving water, air and land around. We follow a raindrop through the water cycle, then see what happens when there is too much (flood) or too little (drought). The monsoon happens because land heats faster than the sea, so moist sea air rushes in. We count the seconds between lightning and thunder to tell how far away a storm is. We learn how earthquakes shake the ground and how in 2004 some Andaman island communities reportedly escaped the tsunami using traditional knowledge of the sea. And we ask whether 'natural disasters' are fully natural: building on riverbeds or cutting forests can make floods far worse.
topics.oneness: Rain, rivers and my body's water are the same water. Is a flood something happening to us or with us?

res.title: India Meteorological Department: today's weather
A stepwell (e.g. Chand Baori, Rajasthan) or a local lake

topics.name: Human impact on the environment
sub: Humans change land (forests → farms and cities), air (smoke), water (plastic, sewage) and climate (burning coal and petrol adds carbon dioxide)
Other animals change environments too (elephants, termites, earthworms, beavers), but humans at a huge scale
Good changes: Jadav Payeng planted a whole forest on a river island; the Chipko movement
Are humans part of nature or outside it?
topics.summary: Every living thing changes its surroundings: earthworms make soil, elephants clear paths, termites build towers. Humans do the same, but at a scale that now changes the whole planet's air, water and weather. We walk the neighbourhood spotting human-made changes, catch dust from the air on a sticky card, and feel how a road is hotter than a tree's shade. We meet people who changed things for the better: Jadav Payeng, the 'Forest Man of India', planted a forest bigger than many towns, and the women of the Chipko movement hugged trees to save them. We discuss honestly that people disagree about how fast to change things and which solutions are best.
topics.oneness: If I am part of nature, is damaging nature damaging myself?

res.title: StoryWeaver: Jadav and the Tree-Place
The Elephant Whisperers (2022)
Our Planet (2019)

topics.name: Waste: reduce & manage
sub: Nature has no waste: a fallen leaf becomes soil
Kinds of waste: wet, dry, hazardous, e-waste
Where waste goes: landfills, burning, recycling, oceans
Plastic can last hundreds of years
Refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle; composting
India's kabadiwala recycling system
topics.summary: In a forest nothing is wasted: leaves, dead animals and dung all become food for something else. Only humans make things nature cannot easily take back, like plastic that lasts for centuries. We find out what our own family throws away in a week, sort it into wet, dry and hazardous, and bury a banana peel, a paper and a plastic bag to dig up after 3 weeks. We meet India's kabadiwalas, who quietly recycle huge amounts, and old habits like turning sarees into quilts. We also learn an uncomfortable fact: only a small part of all plastic ever made has been recycled, and experts argue about whether recycling is the real answer.
topics.oneness: If nature has no waste, is waste a human idea? Can we live like a forest?

res.title: Arvind Gupta Toys: toys from trash

topics.name: Other life inside me
sub: Trillions of microbes live in and on us: roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells
Gut, skin and mouth each have their own communities
They help digest food, make some vitamins and train our defences
Mitochondria, the energy-makers in our cells, were once free-living bacteria
About 8% of our DNA is left over from ancient viruses
topics.summary: You are not just you: you are a walking city. About as many bacterial cells live in and on your body as your own cells (scientists used to say 10 times more, until a 2016 study corrected it). Your gut microbes help digest food and make vitamins; skin microbes guard against germs. Deeper still, the tiny power stations inside every cell, mitochondria, were once separate bacteria that moved in and never left. Lynn Margulis proposed this and was ridiculed for years before scientists accepted it. Even our DNA carries leftover pieces of ancient viruses. So which part is 'me'?
topics.oneness: If half the cells in my body are not 'mine', and my energy comes from ancient bacteria, what is 'I'?

res.title: Khan Academy: cells and microbes (older kids, parent prep)

topics.name: My genes
sub: Every cell carries instructions (DNA), like a recipe book
Half from each biological parent; why siblings differ
All life uses the same DNA 'letters'; we share many genes with bananas, flies and mice
Genes are not destiny: food, care and surroundings switch genes on and off
History: Mendel's peas; Rosalind Franklin's photo; Har Gobind Khorana and the genetic code
topics.summary: Inside almost every cell is a long coded message called DNA, a recipe book for building and running a body. We extract real DNA from strawberries and see the white strands. Half our recipes come from each biological parent, mixed in a new way, which is why siblings look alike but different. All living things use the same four DNA letters, so we share many genes even with bananas. We meet Mendel, a monk whose pea experiments were ignored for 34 years; Rosalind Franklin, whose photo revealed DNA's shape but who got little credit; and Har Gobind Khorana, born in Punjab, who won a Nobel Prize for cracking how DNA's code works. And we learn that genes are not destiny: what we eat, how we live and how we are cared for changes which genes are used.
topics.oneness: If a banana and I share the same code, are we written in the same language by the same author?

res.title: Strawberry DNA extraction (lesson card)

topics.name: Where humans came from
sub: Life changed over billions of years (evolution): fish → amphibians → reptiles → mammals → primates → humans, a branching tree, not a ladder
Darwin and Wallace: natural selection
Other humans: Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans; Homo sapiens appear about 300,000 years ago in Africa
Many of us carry a little Neanderthal DNA
People reached India tens of thousands of years ago; Bhimbetka rock shelters
topics.summary: We follow our family line back through time: fish that crawled onto land, early mammals scurrying under dinosaurs, tree-climbing primates, and many kinds of humans, several of them alive at the same time. Darwin and Wallace explained how living things slowly change: those best suited to their surroundings survive and pass on their traits. We see that evolution is a branching bush, not a ladder, and that new fossils keep pushing dates back. We visit (in pictures or in person) Bhimbetka's rock paintings, among the oldest human art in India. Then we compare this with the Dashavatara: Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (half-lion, half-human), Vamana (small human), then full humans. Many people see in this order a story that parallels evolution.
topics.oneness: If all life is one family tree, is there anyone who is not my relative?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh)

topics.name: What's common between me and other life?
sub: Me & a dog: mammals, backbone, the same organs, hair, milk, feelings
Me & a bird: backbone, lungs, a 4-chambered heart
Me & a fish: backbone; early embryos look alike
Me & a tree: cells, DNA, using energy, water
Me & a mushroom: closer relatives than plants
Me & bacteria: the same DNA code and energy molecule
Differences too
topics.summary: We play detective comparing ourselves with other beings, one at a time. A dog shares our skeleton plan, organs, fur-like hair, milk-feeding and clearly feels joy and fear. A bird has a 4-chambered heart like ours. A tree breathes at the level of its cells, carries DNA and is made of cells like us. Even bacteria run on the same genetic code and energy molecule. The deeper we look, the longer the 'same' list grows. We also hear the 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, in which scientists stated that many animals, including birds and octopuses, are conscious, and the 2024 New York Declaration, which says even insects might be.
topics.oneness: 'Tat tvam asi': you are that. When does 'same' become 'one'?

res.title: My Octopus Teacher (2020)

topics.name: Our closest cousins
sub: Great apes: chimpanzees and bonobos (closest; about 98–99% similar DNA), gorillas, orangutans
Monkeys and other primates
India's only ape: the hoolock gibbon (Northeast)
Shared: tools, emotions, play, laughter, culture
Jane Goodall: chimps use tools
topics.summary: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives; we shared an ancestor several million years ago. When Jane Goodall saw a chimp stripping a twig to fish for termites, scientists had believed tool-making was what made humans unique. Her mentor Louis Leakey said we must now 'redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Chimps laugh, mourn, make up after fights and have local traditions. India has its own ape, the hoolock gibbon, singing in northeastern forests. We tape our thumbs to see why our hands matter, and ask: what, if anything, makes humans special?
topics.oneness: Every 'only humans can…' claim has been challenged. Is the line between us and them real?

res.title: Jane Goodall documentaries (e.g. Jane, 2017)

topics.name: My family history
sub: Family tree (3 generations); 'family' = the people who raise and love me (inclusive of adopted, single-parent and other families)
Traits that run in families: face, height, hair, handedness
Fingerprints: unique, even for identical twins
Stories, languages, places, recipes
How long people lived then vs now
Blood groups and family illnesses: parent-led and kept light
topics.summary: Every child is the newest page in a very long story. We build a family tree, interview a grandparent or elder, collect photos and stories, and look at what is shared: a nose, a laugh, a love of cooking. We take fingerprints and discover that no two people, not even identical twins, have the same ones. We learn that in 1947 people in India lived on average only about 32 years and now about 70, and ask why. For families that wish to, parents can add blood groups and health stories. Families made by adoption or in other ways trace both their 'raised-by' and 'born-from' stories in whatever way feels right.
topics.oneness: My family tree joins every other family tree if I go back far enough. Where does my family end?

topics.name: My body parts
sub: Skin (the largest organ), bones (about 300 at birth, 206 in adults), muscles, heart, lungs, stomach and intestines, brain
How they work together
Why they evolved: forward eyes, gripping thumbs, sweating for long-distance running, goosebumps from furry ancestors, tailbone
The appendix: once called useless, now possibly a store of helpful microbes
topics.summary: We trace the child's body on a big sheet of paper and place cut-out organs inside. We listen to the heart with a home-made stethoscope before and after jumping, blow up a balloon to feel lung power, and build a moving finger from straws and string. Then we ask 'why do I have this?' Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors whose hair stood up; sweating lets humans run for hours; babies are born with about 300 bones that fuse to 206. We learn that science changes its mind: the appendix was called useless for a century and now may be a safe house for helpful gut microbes. Finally we meet another way of seeing the body: Sushruta, an early surgeon who described nose reconstruction, and the yoga and Ayurveda traditions that describe the body differently.
topics.oneness: My heart beats without my asking. Is it 'my' heart, or is it doing its own thing?

res.title: Science centres: Nehru Science Centre Mumbai, Visvesvaraya Museum Bengaluru, National Science Centre Delhi

topics.name: My body's sensors
sub: Beyond the 'five senses': touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, itch, balance, body position (eyes closed), hunger, thirst, full tummy, heartbeat, the urge to breathe
Conscious vs automatic sensing
Senses mix: flavour = taste + smell
Other beings: birds (UV, magnetic field), bees (UV), snakes (heat), sharks (electric fields), bats (echoes), dogs (smell)
Plants sense light, gravity and touch
topics.summary: Aristotle listed five senses over 2000 years ago, and people repeated the list ever since. But your body is covered in sensors: you know where your hand is with your eyes closed, you feel hot and cold, you stay balanced on one foot, you feel hungry, thirsty or that you need the toilet, and a hidden sensor makes you breathe faster when you run. Scientists today count anywhere from about 20 to over 30 senses and still disagree on how to count. We pinch our noses and find apple and potato taste almost the same, because most flavour is smell. Then we meet the superpowers of others: snakes 'see' heat, sharks feel electricity, bats hear their way in the dark, birds feel Earth's magnetism. Even plants sense: roots know which way is down and the touch-me-not folds when touched.
topics.oneness: If a plant senses touch and I sense touch, is sensing the beginning of awareness everywhere?

res.title: What If You Had Animal Eyes?, Sandra Markle

topics.name: How do I think?
sub: The brain: about 86 billion neurons sending signals
Thinking = patterns of signals; learning changes connections
Memory: short-term and long-term; sleep helps memory; memories change each time we recall them
Emotions affect thinking
Other thinkers: crows, octopuses; even brainless slime moulds solve mazes
The hard question: how does the brain make experience?
topics.summary: Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells passing tiny electric and chemical signals; every time you learn something new, the connections change. We play memory games and discover tricks that help (stories, pictures, a 'memory palace' walk through the house) and learn that sleep is when the brain files memories. Surprisingly, a memory changes a little each time you remember it. Thinking isn't only human: crows plan, octopuses solve puzzles, and a slime mould with no brain at all can find the shortest path through a maze. Then the biggest mystery: nobody knows how signals in the brain become the feeling of being you. Some scientists say the mind is what the brain does; Vedanta says consciousness comes first and the brain is something that appears within it.
topics.oneness: Who is watching my thoughts? Is the watcher a thought too?

topics.name: Getting sick, getting hurt & getting well
sub: Why we get sick: germs (bacteria, viruses), not enough food or sleep, allergies
The body's defences: skin, mucus, fever, white blood cells, antibodies, immune memory (how vaccines work)
Hygiene habits: handwashing (20 seconds), teeth, bathing, clean water and food, covering coughs
Getting hurt: cuts, burns, falls, electric shock; electricity safety at home
Healing: scabs, rest
Are 'I' and 'my body' different?
topics.summary: We learn that the body is a fortress: skin is the wall, mucus is a sticky trap, fever is the body turning up the heat on germs, and white blood cells are guards who remember invaders so they can fight faster next time (which is how vaccines work). Glitter 'germs' show why handwashing matters, and bread touched by washed vs unwashed hands grows very different mould. We tell the story of Dr Semmelweis, who told doctors to wash their hands in the 1840s and was mocked; years later germ theory proved him right. We learn home safety, especially electricity: water and electricity never mix, never touch sockets or bare wires, and never touch someone being shocked; switch off first. Finally the question: we say 'help my body heal'. Who is helping whom? Am I my body, or something more?
topics.oneness: When I say 'my body', who is the 'I' that owns it?

res.title: Germs Make Me Sick!, Melvin Berger

topics.name: What is food?
sub: Food = building material + energy + helpers (vitamins, minerals) + water
Digestion breaks food down: proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → sugars, fats → fatty acids
All life uses the same ~20 amino acids, DNA code and energy molecule (ATP)
So why so many foods? Different bodies have different tools (teeth, enzymes, gut microbes)
Plants make their own food from light; food chains
Food for different beings: cows (helped by microbes), spiders, plants, fungi
topics.summary: We chew a piece of plain roti for two minutes and it starts tasting sweet: saliva is already breaking starch into sugar. Digestion is a giant breaking-down factory: proteins become amino acids, carbohydrates become sugars, fats become fatty acids, and the body rebuilds them into itself. Amazingly, every living thing builds itself from the same 20 or so amino acids. So why does a cow eat grass, a spider eat flies and a plant eat sunlight? Because each has different tools: a cow's stomach is full of microbes that break down grass, which we cannot do. We also learn that nutrition science keeps changing its mind: fat was the villain, then sugar, and eggs went from bad to fine.
topics.oneness: 'Annam Brahma': food is the Absolute. When I eat a mango, does the mango become me, or do I become a little more mango?

res.title: StoryWeaver: food stories

topics.name: Energy beyond food
sub: Sunlight: plants make sugar from light (photosynthesis); we make vitamin D in sunlight; warmth
Air: oxygen helps cells release energy from food; we breathe out carbon dioxide
Water: most of the body is water; every cell works in it
Life without sunlight: deep-sea vents where bacteria make food from chemicals (chemosynthesis); tubeworms
Microbes that 'breathe' nitrate or sulphate instead of oxygen; life in boiling springs, ice and deep rock
Tardigrades survive extremes
topics.summary: Food is only one kind of fuel. Plants catch sunlight and turn it into sugar; that sugar feeds almost everything else, including us. Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, like a slow fire, and we breathe out carbon dioxide. A plant left in a dark box turns pale, and a candle under a jar goes out when its oxygen runs low. Then we dive to the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight has ever reached, and find whole communities living on chemicals from hot volcanic vents. Some microbes breathe sulphate instead of oxygen, some live in boiling water or deep inside rocks, and tiny tardigrades can survive drying out and even the vacuum of space. Life is far stranger and more flexible than the textbook picture.
topics.oneness: If all my energy started as sunlight, am I a little bit of the Sun, walking around?
